title: Bathing before prayer
hookLine: washing the body before prayer, as the Gursikh routine describes
tomorrow: how much prayer fits into a morning that's already running late?

lines: A COLD SPLASH, A HOT SHOWER.
cards: Water on skin does something nothing else does. The first cold splash at the sink, the hot shower after a long day, rain you didn't plan for: the body wakes up all at once.
In the Sikh morning, water comes right after the alarm. Guru Ram Das, on ang 305, puts it in one line with the early hour: rise early, make the effort, bathe, and dip in the pool of nectar.

teach.b: The word is ishnaan, bathing. It's plain and physical: Sikhs who keep the morning routine wash the whole body before the banis, and keep the hair clean and combed under the turban or scarf.
But listen to how Guru Nanak talks about water in Japji's twentieth pauri.
In paraphrase: when the hands, feet and body are dirty, water washes the dust away. When clothes are soiled, soap washes them clean.
When the mind is stained with wrongdoing, it's washed by love of the Name. Two washings, one after the other. Water for the body; the Name for the mind.
And the next pauri pushes further.

Pilgrimages, austerities, charity earn only a sesame seed of honor, it says in paraphrase; the one who hears, trusts and loves bathes at the shrine within. So the bath at dawn isn't a ritual that cleans you for God.
It's a body getting ready to sit still, while the real washing happens inside.
Clean body, clear mind: the first is the doorway to the second.

how: Sikhs who keep the Gursikh morning routine rise early, bathe the whole body and wash and comb the hair before the morning banis; Gurbani pairs this outer bath with the inner washing of the Name.

o: the sweet food shared after prayer at the gurdwara
a pilgrimage made to a holy river on a festival
bathing: washing the body before morning prayer

p: washed by love of the Name

s: for Sikhs, the morning bath makes you clean enough for God
Japji says water washes the body; the mind is washed by love of the Name.
Guru Ram Das puts rising early and bathing in the same line
ang 305: rise early, make the effort, bathe, dip in the pool of nectar.
Japji says pilgrimage alone earns only a sesame seed of honor
hearing, trusting and loving: that's the bath at the shrine within.

games.q: a cousin showers carefully every morning but rushes through prayer, saying 'clean body, done.' what does Japji's twentieth pauri add?
o: water washes off the dust; a stained mind is washed by love of the Name.
the shower counts as the prayer, so rushing the rest of it is fine.
a cold shower is required before prayer, or the washing doesn't count.
games.why: Japji names two washings, one after the other. the bath readies the body; the Name does the deeper cleaning.

practice: Go to the nearest sink, or wait for your next one, and wash your hands slowly: cool water over the backs, the palms, the wrists. Feel the water on your skin and notice it leaving.
Then sit with dry hands, and let the quiet do the other washing.

wordCard.voice: Ishnaan. Bathing: water for the body at dawn, and, in Japji, the Name washing the mind.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ishnaan, bathing; the morning bath of the Gursikh routine.

carryVoice: Your line: clean body, clear mind. One washing opens the door to the other. Day done.
